expansion:
A. Temporal artery biopsy is the keyed answer. This presentation is characteristic of giant cell arteritis causing arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy: acute painless monocular visual loss with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, constitutional symptoms and proximal stiffness. Temporal artery biopsy demonstrates the vasculitic arterial inflammation and is the gold-standard confirmatory test (not taken from the course material). The acute-visual-loss lecture presents a similar elderly woman with visual loss, headache, fatigue and weight loss (L31,32, slide 20), and diagnoses “Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy” (L31,32, slide 23). However, it explicitly states that the management slide contains “Nothing ... about the temporal artery, about biopsy, about ESR/CRP” (L31,32, slide 24), so the biopsy fact is not taught in the lecture. The lecture also records that “jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, polymyalgia” are “not printed” (L31,32, slide 31), despite these being decisive clues in this question.

B. Carotid endarterectomy is surgery to remove atherosclerotic plaque from a carotid artery, principally to reduce stroke risk in selected carotid stenosis; it neither confirms giant cell arteritis nor samples the affected temporal artery (not taken from the course material).

C. Optic nerve sheath fenestration is a procedure used to protect vision in selected cases of raised intracranial pressure, especially idiopathic intracranial hypertension. It is not a diagnostic test for giant cell arteritis and does not establish the cause of this patient’s optic neuropathy (not taken from the course material).

D. A cranial burr hole is a neurosurgical opening used, for example, to drain certain intracranial haemorrhages or obtain cranial access. It has no diagnostic role in confirming giant cell arteritis (not taken from the course material).
objective: Recognise temporal artery biopsy as the gold-standard confirmatory investigation for suspected giant cell arteritis.
